title: When Folding Goes Wrong
principle: The cell has helpers that stop proteins folding wrong.

t: Sometimes a protein folds the wrong way. Sometimes the wrong shape is stickier than the right one.
Folding usually finds the right answer. When it does not, the misfolded form is occasionally more stable than the correct one — and then it does not go back.
sub: And then it is very hard to undo.
A wrong shape that is more stable than the right shape is a different kind of problem from a mistake.

question: What is the danger of a protein folding into a sticky wrong shape?
Why is a stable misfolded conformation dangerous beyond the loss of one protein's function?
options: It sticks to others and they clump together
It turns into a different protein
stages.outcome: It sticks to others and they clump together
note: Commit. The answer is why a single misfolded molecule can matter at all.

t: Fold this one and see how easy it is to get stuck somewhere that is nearly right but not right.
Fold this chain to its best shape. Notice how many arrangements are close to the answer without being it.
goal: You got there. But there were plenty of nearly-right shapes on the way.
Found it. The point is how many almost-right arrangements you passed through — a real chain has vastly more.

t: Find this one's best fold. Then count how many bends you needed, and think about a real protein with three hundred beads.
Reach the optimum, then consider the scaling. This chain has 12 residues and a handful of moves; a real protein has hundreds, and cannot search them all.
goal: Found it — and you had to search. A real protein cannot search, so it must not need to.

Levinthal's paradox in miniature: a 100-residue chain sampling every conformation would take longer than the universe has existed, yet folding takes milliseconds. The resolution is that folding is a funnel, not a search — the landscape is biased toward the native state from everywhere on it.

t: The cell has helpers that stop proteins folding wrong. They are called chaperones.
Chaperone proteins bind newly made chains and prevent them from aggregating while they fold.
Chaperones do not specify the fold — they suppress the wrong outcomes, mainly by keeping exposed hydrophobic surfaces from finding each other.

The distinction matters: a chaperone raises the yield of the native state without adding information to it. Anfinsen still holds — the sequence determines the structure — and the chaperone only improves the odds of getting there without aggregating on the way.
sub: And a cell can throw away the ones that still come out wrong.
Beyond that there is quality control: persistently misfolded proteins are tagged and destroyed.
Ubiquitin tagging marks a protein for the proteasome. Roughly a third of newly made proteins are destroyed almost immediately, which is a startling amount of deliberate waste.

That waste is the price of speed. Translation running fast enough to be useful produces a substantial defective fraction, and it is cheaper to destroy them than to slow everything down — the same fidelity-versus-rate trade you met in replication.

q: Why is a sticky misfolded protein dangerous?
Why does misfolding cause disease beyond the loss of function?
options: It makes others fold wrong too, and they pile up
It stops the cell making new proteins
It uses up all the water
why: The wrong shape has sticky bits on the outside. It grabs others, they clump, and the clumps get bigger — losing one protein would not matter much, but a growing pile does.

The misfolded form templates the same misfolding in normal copies, so the problem grows rather than staying constant, and the aggregates themselves are toxic. Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and type 2 diabetes all involve protein aggregation.

Amyloid is a cross-β structure that is thermodynamically very stable and grows by recruiting monomers onto its ends. That is self-templating — which is why prion diseases are transmissible without any nucleic acid at all, a claim that took Prusiner a decade to get accepted.

t: Some of the hardest diseases to treat are protein-folding problems.

Cystic fibrosis is largely a folding disease: the commonest mutation produces a channel that works but never reaches the cell surface because quality control destroys it as misfolded. Drugs that help it fold correctly — correctors — treat the underlying defect rather than the symptoms, which is why they changed the prognosis so sharply.
